title: Moving Up (1)

jokes.text: Can't believe Michael Bay spent a billion dollars of his own money to build that for The Rock.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are looking at Alcatraz from the plane/ferry, taking in the famous landmark.
jokes.punchline: Leslie confidently and sincerely believes Michael Bay built Alcatraz as a movie set for 'The Rock,' conflating the film with reality.
jokes.explanation: This joke works beautifully because it's deeply character-specific to Leslie — her encyclopedic but often hilariously misapplied knowledge. The confidence with which she states an absurd falsehood as fact is Leslie's comic DNA. High character integration because this could only be Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, Alcatraz! Michael Bay must have spent a fortune building this as a movie set.

jokes.text: I couldn't tell, 'cause you had that mask thing over your eyes.
jokes.setup: Ben says 'You weren't trying to sleep, were you?' about Leslie reciting The Rock from memory on the plane.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has no idea she was being inconsiderate — she genuinely thought the sleep mask meant Ben couldn't hear her.
jokes.explanation: A tight, well-structured beat. Leslie's obliviousness is funny and character-true. The economy of the single line does a lot of work revealing her blissful lack of self-awareness. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, I've been thinking. On the flight to DC, I could recite the entire script of 'Braveheart' to entertain you.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Please don't.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Too late. I already did it. Twice.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I was asleep. You recited it to an unconscious person and a very uncomfortable flight attendant.

jokes.text: 'What happens at a National Parks Conference is compiled and emailed to you in a PDF the following Monday.'
jokes.setup: Leslie begins the classic 'What happens in Vegas, stays in Vegas' setup: 'And you know what they say...'
jokes.punchline: The punchline is a hyper-bureaucratic, utterly unglamorous version of the phrase — a PDF emailed on Monday — perfectly encapsulating Leslie's world.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: a universal setup (Vegas phrase) subverted by a hyper-specific, bureaucratic punchline that reveals everything about Leslie's world in a single sentence. 'Compiled and emailed to you in a PDF the following Monday' is a masterclass in comedic specificity. Deeply character-integrated — only Leslie Knope would say this with full sincerity. The talking-head delivery makes it land even harder. Highly quotable and earns 9+ across the board.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas? No. I'm going to file a detailed trip report with the Parks Department, cross-reference it with the municipal code, and create a comprehensive binder documenting every single thing that happened.

jokes.text: They give tours. / Yeah. That's exactly how they'll be expecting me to try to break in.
jokes.setup: Two characters are trying to figure out how to get into Alcatraz.
jokes.punchline: Andy rejects the official tour as a method of entry because it's 'exactly how they'll be expecting' him — as if he's planning a heist rather than being a tourist.
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Andy. His action-movie logic applied to mundane situations is a reliable comedic engine, and 'that's exactly how they'll be expecting me to try to break in' is a genuinely funny inversion of the obvious. Good economy, good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Why don't you just take a tour?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A tour? April, that's exactly what they'd expect me to do. It's too obvious. They're probably waiting for me to take a tour. I need to come in through the loading dock, bypass the main entrance, maybe rappel down from the roof.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's a tour.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A DECOY tour, April. They're three steps ahead of me.

jokes.text: This is the hardest I've worked on anything since... [pause] Wow. I've never worked hard on anything. What a cool life!
jokes.setup: Tom says he's making sure he gets every detail right on his restaurant — 'This is the hardest I've worked on anything since...' implying a serious memory is coming.
jokes.punchline: He realizes mid-sentence he has NO previous example, and instead of being embarrassed, celebrates this as a positive: 'What a cool life!'
jokes.explanation: A top-tier joke in the episode. The misdirection setup (expecting a self-serious memory) pivots into Tom discovering his own laziness in real time, then genuinely celebrating it. 'What a cool life!' is the perfect Tom Haverford capper — his shamelessness is his superpower. Excellent structure with the mid-sentence beat and the talking-head format making it land perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is some of the hardest work I've ever done. Well, actually, no it isn't. I've never done hard work. This is great!

jokes.text: They're not even done painting that sign. It says 'Tom's bi.'
jokes.setup: Someone points out they're not ready to open because the sign isn't finished.
jokes.punchline: The unfinished sign only reads 'Tom's bi' — a truncated and unintentionally suggestive partial word.
jokes.explanation: A solid visual/wordplay gag. The unfinished sign joke is a sitcom standard, but 'Tom's bi' is a genuinely funny specific truncation. Not deeply character-integrated but gets a good laugh from the audience.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm totally wigging out about this restaurant opening. I mean, I'm not Kristen, but I'm definitely losing my hair over this.

jokes.text: Actually, no, that's good. We're ready.
jokes.setup: Someone says the unfinished sign reading 'Tom's bi' is a problem.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately pivots to accepting it as fine — implying he's okay with the accidental messaging.
jokes.explanation: A quick callback beat that extends the sign joke. Tom's nonchalance about the accidental double meaning is on-brand for his 'any publicity is good publicity' persona. Economy is excellent — it's a two-word punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look at that sign. It says 'Tom's Bistro' but the 'Bistro' part fell off.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So right now it just says 'Tom's Bi.' I'm not gonna lie, that's a pretty aggressive way to come out.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But you know what? I'm keeping it. Free advertising.

jokes.text: 'This little Italian restaurant will put McDonald's out of business' on three. One, two, three! ...rise from hell fire!
jokes.setup: Tom leads a team chant to build morale for the soft opening.
jokes.punchline: Someone in the background shouts '...rise from hell fire!' instead of the agreed line — a completely unhinged non-sequitur that suggests the chaos beneath the surface.
jokes.explanation: The mismatch between the earnest corporate-style pep talk and the unhinged employee shouting about hellfire is delightfully absurd. It also seeds the chaos to come in the restaurant. Good structural surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A parks bureaucrat? That's like... that's like a bad boy.

jokes.text: Lester Kanopf? / Come on, guys, get it together.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just finished an ambitious monologue about the week ahead; she's at what appears to be a check-in desk.
jokes.punchline: Her name is mispronounced/mixed up as 'Lester Kanopf' — immediately deflating her grand self-presentation. She shakes it off with exasperation.
jokes.explanation: A serviceable deflation gag — Leslie's grandiosity undercut by a mundane bureaucratic error. Works but is fairly standard sitcom business.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What do they do?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have no idea.

jokes.text: Liam Bonneville? The Department of the Interior's resident bad boy? Well, now you've got my attention. Let me go grab my autograph book.
jokes.setup: Grant mentions that Liam Bonneville will be at lunch.
jokes.punchline: Leslie reacts to a bureaucrat from the Department of the Interior as if he's a rock star — complete with the phrase 'resident bad boy' and grabbing an autograph book.
jokes.explanation: Pure Leslie Knope — her celebrity is entirely defined by the civil service world. 'The Department of the Interior's resident bad boy' is a brilliantly specific oxymoron. Only Leslie would have an autograph book for this. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, you have a barber chair in your office? That's amazing! How much does a haircut cost here?

dialogue.speaker: Tech Executive
dialogue.line: It's free for all employees. We believe in work-life balance and—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Free?! Dude, I'm in. When can I get a cut?

jokes.text: And what exactly does Gryzzl do? [Talking head] No idea.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains they're going to pitch Pawnee to Gryzzl, a tech company. Ben asks what they do.
jokes.punchline: Cut to talking head — Ben simply says 'No idea' with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: The cut to talking head with a two-word answer is structurally efficient and satirizes the tech company mystique (and civic ignorance). Economy is near-perfect. The abruptness of the cut is what sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Pawnee isn't as big as Shreveport or Akron.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Those are my aspirational comparison cities.

jokes.text: Six months ago, I was working in a taco truck. Now, I own one-third of the Portland Trailblazers.
jokes.setup: A Gryzzl employee is describing the company's meteoric rise.
jokes.punchline: The taco truck to NBA ownership trajectory is designed to sound inspirational but instead underscores the absurdity of Silicon Valley wealth concentration.
jokes.explanation: Good satirical observation on tech-boom culture. The specificity of 'one-third of the Portland Trailblazers' elevates it from generic. The obliviousness of the character makes it funnier — he thinks this is normal.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl exec
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl exec
dialogue.line: Nah, bro.

jokes.text: So, you can just get your hair cut in the lobby at Gryzzl, huh? [Beat — Andy gets up and cuts someone's hair]
jokes.setup: Andy learns that Gryzzl employees can do whatever they want in the work collective.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately asks if he can cut someone's hair, is told 'if that's how you want to flow,' and proceeds to do exactly that — presumably on a stranger.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Andy — his complete lack of filter and instant opportunism. The 'go get it' callback from whoever he's with seals it. The physical comedy of him cutting a stranger's hair at a business meeting is very on-brand.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Proudly announces he only made 12 mistakes

jokes.text: Sure, obviously, we're no Akron. I mean, we're more like Dayton. But with your help, we can become Toledo.
jokes.setup: Gryzzl says they're focused on bigger cities like Shreveport and Akron.
jokes.punchline: Ben's pitch degrades in real time — from 'we're no Akron' to 'we're like Dayton' to the aspiration of becoming Toledo. Each city is less impressive than the last.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely excellent joke. The escalating descent from Akron to Dayton to Toledo as an aspirational endpoint is funny as a piece of writing, and it works because the structure keeps going one step further down than you expect. Ben's earnestness makes it land. The specificity of Ohio cities is perfect comedy geography. Near anchor-quality at the 8.0 level.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you're so good at woodworking, you should change your name to Dwayne 'The Wood' Johnson.

jokes.text: Ben, we don't like to say the word 'no'... No. ...at this company.
jokes.setup: A Gryzzl employee begins explaining their company philosophy of never saying 'no.'
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately says 'No' during the pause, completely undercutting the speech before it's even finished.
jokes.explanation: A structurally elegant joke — the pause is engineered perfectly so Ben's interruption of 'No' lands before the setup is complete. It satirizes both corporate-speak and Ben's impatience. Economy is excellent. The timing is everything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I need chairs. Like, really quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You want chairs? Jameson Furniture Works, 1987. They made the best chairs in the region. Everyone knows that.

jokes.text: 'Nah, bro.' / How is that better?
jokes.setup: The Gryzzl employee says instead of 'no' they say 'Nah, bro.'
jokes.punchline: Ben's deadpan 'How is that better?' is the perfect straight-man response.
jokes.explanation: The callback extends the previous joke well. 'Nah, bro' as a corporate philosophy euphemism is a sharp satirical observation, and Ben's straight-man response is perfect. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I've never asked you for anything. Today.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's because you've only worked here since this morning.

jokes.text: Dwayne 'The Rock' Swanson.
jokes.setup: Tom finds Ron working on the third floor he has secretly renovated.
jokes.punchline: Tom greets him as 'Dwayne The Rock Swanson' — a callback to the opening Rock/Alcatraz joke plus Ron's stoic physicality.
jokes.explanation: A clever callback to the opening Michael Bay/The Rock joke. Also works as a standalone description of Ron's physical gravitas. 'The Rock Swanson' is a genuinely funny portmanteau. Good economy — just three words do a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I made it myself. I took a photo of Rebecca at a concert, I scanned it into my computer, I enhanced the colors, I printed it out on poster paper, and then I laminated it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Twice.

jokes.text: All right, I can't keep this facade up any longer. I need a favor.
jokes.setup: Tom has been lavishing Ron with compliments about his renovation work.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately drops the flattery act and reveals he only came to ask for a favor — the compliments were entirely transactional.
jokes.explanation: A reliable sitcom beat — character drops pretense immediately. Tom's shamelessness is on-brand. The speed of the reveal (he can barely maintain the facade) is what makes it funny. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're reading my proposal? Oh my god, this is so exciting!

dialogue.speaker: Liam
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's... words on paper.

jokes.text: Who do you think I am, Thomas Hucker?
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ron to speed up making his chairs.
jokes.punchline: Ron is offended by the request to rush, and invokes 'Thomas Hucker' — presumably a notorious rushed craftsman — as the insult he's not going to accept.
jokes.explanation: The joke works because 'Thomas Hucker' is clearly an invented/obscure craftsman whose name means nothing to the audience, which makes Ron's confidence in the reference funnier. Pure Ron Swanson — his craftsman's code expressed through an absurd reference no one else would make.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Can I... can I high-five you?

dialogue.speaker: Michelle Obama
dialogue.line: Of course.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God. Oh my God.

jokes.text: Please, Ron? I've never asked you for anything today.
jokes.setup: Tom is begging Ron to rush the chairs.
jokes.punchline: Tom's pleading is that he's 'never asked for anything today' — acknowledging implicitly that he asks for things constantly, just not yet today.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The modification of 'I've never asked you for anything' to 'I've never asked you for anything today' is a perfectly timed self-own. It simultaneously begs and confesses Tom's entire character — he asks for things constantly and knows it. Maximum funny per word, excellent structure, deeply character-specific. Quotable and rewatch-worthy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I was really hoping you'd be on that.

jokes.text: I've read all of your papers, and I had your poster on my wall when I was a kid. / What poster? / I made a poster of you by blowing up your picture from the National Parks newsletter. I cut out your face and made it look like you were dunking over Charles Barkley.
jokes.setup: Leslie fan-girls over Rebecca Varuvian, a National Parks official.
jokes.punchline: The poster reveal escalates from nerdy-but-understandable (blowing up a newsletter photo) to full absurdity (cutting out her face to make it look like she was dunking over Charles Barkley).
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character comedy. The escalation from 'newsletter photo' to 'dunking over Charles Barkley' is perfectly structured — each reveal is funnier than the last. Only Leslie Knope would do this, and the specificity of Charles Barkley (not just 'a basketball player') makes it memorable. High quotability. One of the episode's strongest moments.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, Michelle Obama? How is that not the first thing you told me?

jokes.text: It wasn't bad. / Liam Bonneville read my proposal. Wow.
jokes.setup: Liam Bonneville says Leslie's proposal 'wasn't bad.'
jokes.punchline: Leslie is visibly overwhelmed that a bureaucrat from the Interior department read her work — treating it as the highest praise imaginable.
jokes.explanation: Works as a continuation of the 'Leslie's heroes are bureaucrats' joke. The contrast between Bonneville's withholding praise and Leslie's awe is well-executed. Functional but relies on an established pattern.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, so you met the First Lady before you met the parks official?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And the parks official flustered you more?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, yes. So much more.

jokes.text: Are you nodding because you agree with me? / Yes. / I do agree with you. / I agree with you on all things. Throughout history. Until the end of time, forever.
jokes.setup: Michelle Obama is agreeing with Leslie's excitement about the national parks.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's agreement escalates absurdly — from a sincere 'yes' to 'throughout history, until the end of time, forever' — as she completely loses the ability to have a normal conversation.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully escalating moment of character comedy. Leslie's total inability to play it cool with heroes is a season-long comic engine, and 'throughout history, until the end of time, forever' is the kind of over-the-top escalation that defines her. Michelle Obama's patience makes it funnier. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why are there all these disturbing photos on the menu?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, those are pictures of my dog's medical condition.

jokes.text: Great work! I'm sorry I'm talking so loud! I'm getting louder and now I can't stop! My apologies!
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to have a conversation with Michelle Obama and is losing control of her volume.
jokes.punchline: She escalates her self-awareness of getting louder while continuing to get louder — unable to stop even as she apologizes.
jokes.explanation: A great physical/verbal comedy escalation. The joke is that Leslie is aware of her problem but powerless to stop it — self-consciousness making things worse. Amy Poehler's delivery sells this enormously. The structure of getting louder while apologizing for getting louder is solid comedic architecture.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: This is Larry's worst mistake ever. And this is a guy who once stapled his tie to his chest.

jokes.text: Can I high-five you? / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Leslie is barely holding it together in front of Michelle Obama.
jokes.punchline: She asks permission to high-five — the most Leslie Knope possible interaction with the First Lady.
jokes.explanation: The polite request for a high-five — rather than just doing it — is perfectly Leslie. Economy is excellent. The awkward formality of asking permission before celebrating is a good character beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The joints weren't mortised properly, the wood grain wasn't running in the same direction on all four legs, and the finish was uneven. It's an embarrassment.

jokes.text: I thought he was gonna be on it. / Yeah. Anyway...
jokes.setup: Andy apparently rode or sent something down a steep San Francisco street and is impressed by how fast it went.
jokes.punchline: He thought he was going to be ON the thing going down the hill — implying he planned to ride it — but the camera reveals he just sent it without himself. The 'Yeah. Anyway...' dismissal makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Inferred physical comedy — Andy apparently lost whatever he was going to ride down the San Francisco hills. The casual aftermath ('Yeah. Anyway.') is funnier than if it had been played big. Character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so here's what we do. We tell Gryzzl that Pawnee is the perfect place for their new headquarters because of our natural resources, our central location, and our workforce. Then we get them to invest in the community, create jobs, boost the economy. And by the time they realize they've been conned, they'll have made so many friends here that they won't even care. Because friendship is the real treasure.

jokes.text: Liam Bonneville has me in a tizzy!
jokes.setup: Leslie has just made a major life decision — to take the Chicago job.
jokes.punchline: In explaining her emotional state, she cites 'Liam Bonneville has me in a tizzy' — a mild-mannered bureaucrat from the Interior department is her emotional disruption.
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the Liam Bonneville running thread — a bureaucrat has destabilized Leslie Knope the way a celebrity crush would destabilize a normal person. 'In a tizzy' combined with 'Liam Bonneville' is a very funny pairing. Good callback to establish character.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm setting up a WiFi network for the neighborhood. I'm calling it 'Ben's Broadband Legacy.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Years from now, people will remember me every time they connect to the internet.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A lasting monument to my generosity and civic contribution.

jokes.text: No. Can't I just stay in the back and spit in people's food like we planned?
jokes.setup: Tom asks April to handle service at the soft opening.
jokes.punchline: April reveals there was apparently a prior agreement for her to spit in food — and she prefers that arrangement.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential April Ludgate. The phrase 'like we planned' is what elevates this — suggesting it wasn't a rebellious protest but an agreed-upon arrangement, which is even darker and funnier. The casual delivery makes it land hard. Excellent character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, alchemists were abolished in the Third Age of Rethgar when the Council of Mages determined that transmutation violated the Fundamental Laws of Magic. You'd be a thaumaturgist at best, which is completely different.

jokes.text: The sawdust from Ron's chairs is everywhere. My sinuses are on the fritz, and smell is 90% of taste! Maybe 95!
jokes.setup: Craig is trying to taste wine for the soft opening.
jokes.punchline: Craig escalates his complaint about sawdust dust to a precise pseudo-scientific claim about smell and taste, then immediately increases his percentage estimate.
jokes.explanation: Craig's hyperbolic precision ('90%! Maybe 95!') is a reliable laugh. The escalation of the percentage mid-sentence is a good structural choice. Character-specific to Craig's melodrama.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what's the worst case scenario here?

dialogue.speaker: Merger Expert
dialogue.line: The two towns merge, but Pawnee gets completely absorbed. All your parks funding gets redirected to Eagleton. Your department gets dissolved. Everything you've built here disappears.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no. No no no no no. You can't just... Pawnee can't just cease to exist. What about the Harvest Festival? What about Ramsett Park? What about my office?

jokes.text: Oh, geez, I must have given the printer the wrong flash drive. / What is this, a rotten grapefruit? / No, it's my dog's rectum.
jokes.setup: Larry has given menus to a restaurant's soft opening. Tom notices the pictures are wrong.
jokes.punchline: The image Tom first misidentifies as a 'rotten grapefruit' is revealed to be Larry's dog's rectum (because the dog has a growth and he was sending pictures to the vet).
jokes.explanation: A perfectly structured gross-out/Larry joke. The setup (wrong flash drive) → misdirection (rotten grapefruit) → reveal (dog's rectum) is excellent three-step construction. 'No, it's my dog's rectum' is an iconic Larry line — deadpan, mortifying, with enough context (the vet detail) to make it feel earned rather than random. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Fruity AND earthy? How can it be both? That doesn't make any sense! Wine is either fruity OR it's earthy, it can't be both! Pick one!

jokes.text: Fine, but if he raises his voice once, once, I'm out. [Donna reacts to working with Craig]
jokes.setup: Tom assigns Donna and Craig to work as a team for wine tasting.
jokes.punchline: Donna's condition for collaboration is that Craig doesn't raise his voice — a condition that, given Craig's established character, is essentially guaranteed to be violated.
jokes.explanation: A functional character joke that works because the audience knows Craig will immediately violate this condition. The dramatic irony does the work.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I've lost my sense of taste. My taste buds are gone. I'm not a man anymore.

jokes.text: Lord Sheldon has a growth, so we're sending pictures over to the vet. But I guess this isn't good for menus, is it?
jokes.setup: Larry has just revealed the menus have pictures of his dog's rectum on them.
jokes.punchline: His completely underplayed 'I guess this isn't good for menus, is it?' — as if there might be some debate on this point.
jokes.explanation: The understatement of 'I guess this isn't good for menus, is it?' after the dog rectum reveal is perfect Larry. The rhetorical question implies genuine uncertainty and is funnier than if he had just apologized. Excellent economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We need to start from scratch. I'm going to go find some trees.

jokes.text: Larry. Listen to me. This is the worst thing you've ever done.
jokes.setup: Tom surveys the disaster of dog-rectum menus at his restaurant opening.
jokes.punchline: 'This is the worst thing you've ever done' — delivered as a solemn verdict on a fairly mundane accident, while also being probably not true given Larry's history.
jokes.explanation: Serviceable Tom-Larry comedy. The gravity of 'worst thing you've ever done' is funny given Larry's track record, but it's a fairly standard beat in their relationship dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We did it! We won the company together!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, I won it. Solely. By myself.

jokes.text: What was wrong with that one? / It was too perfect. It looked machine-made.
jokes.setup: Tom asks why Ron rejected a perfectly good chair.
jokes.punchline: Ron has rejected a chair for being 'too perfect' — it 'looked machine-made' — because his craftsman's code demands visible imperfection as proof of humanity.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Ron Swanson — his artisanal perfectionism expressed as a rejection of the actual perfect object. The inversion (rejecting something for being too good) is the kind of comic logic that only works because the character is so deeply established. 'It looked machine-made' is a great line.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Pappardelle, rigatoni, fusilli, linguine, fettuccine... Ferrari, Lamborghini, Maserati.

jokes.text: We could tell them that there's buried treasure in Pawnee, and then, after they give us the free WiFi, we tell them that the treasure was love all along.
jokes.setup: Ben says they need to convince Gryzzl that Pawnee is special.
jokes.punchline: Andy's pitch is a children's-book-style bait-and-switch (the treasure was love) presented as an actual business strategy.
jokes.explanation: A very Andy pitch — he's not being cynical, he genuinely thinks this is a viable strategy. The earnestness of 'the treasure was love all along' as a business plan is the joke. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Can I get a menu?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We don't have menus. You eat what we serve you. Also, we take pictures of dog butts here.

jokes.text: Every time someone in Pawnee clicks through a slideshow of American Music Award red carpet sideboob fails, they'll say, 'Thank you, Ben Wyatt.'
jokes.setup: Ben is describing what free WiFi will mean for the residents of Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: His vision of Pawnee's internet use is 'American Music Award red carpet sideboob fails' — revealing both Ben's understanding of his town and the absurd specificity of internet content.
jokes.explanation: The specificity is the joke — not just 'internet content' but 'American Music Award red carpet sideboob fails' as the pinnacle of what Pawnee residents will use WiFi for. Very funny and specific in a way that anchors the show's worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The vet said Champ's tumor is benign. He's gonna be fine.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: They had to drain about two liters of fluid from his abdomen, and his intestines were twisted like a pretzel, but other than that, he's perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Anyway, bon appétit, everyone.

jokes.text: What the hell? They're playing Cones of Dunshire. / Are they playing any games I invented? / Are they throwing dirt into a fan?
jokes.setup: Ben spots Gryzzl employees playing Cones of Dunshire — the elaborate fantasy board game he invented during unemployment.
jokes.punchline: Ben asks if they're playing games he invented, then immediately supplies the only other possible example: 'throwing dirt into a fan.' The contrast between his elaborate board game and this non-game is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ben Wyatt character comedy. The implication that Ben's entire creative output is Cones of Dunshire and 'throwing dirt into a fan' (and he considers both genuine inventions) is deeply funny and character-specific. 'Are they throwing dirt into a fan?' is a great throwaway that recontextualizes Ben's creative history.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My game is really taking off. People can't get enough of it. Everyone wants to get their hands on my pieces.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've had to order more pieces three times this month. The demand for my pieces is absolutely insane.

jokes.text: The key is, you have to throw the dirt into the BACK of the fan.
jokes.setup: Ben mentioned 'throwing dirt into a fan' as one of his game inventions.
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies the strategic nuance of back-of-the-fan vs. front — revealing he has genuinely thought through this non-game.
jokes.explanation: The immediate clarification that there's a correct technique for the dirt-fan game is funnier than the initial mention. Ben's expertise on something this pointless is peak character comedy. The specificity of 'into the back' is what makes it work — he has rules.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't decide if I should stay or go. This is impossible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I blame scientists. If we had cloning technology by now, I could stay AND go. But nooo, we're still waiting.

jokes.text: Yeah, right. And I'm the alchemist of the Hinterlands. / There can't be an alchemist of the Hinterlands. The Hinterlands is a shadow kingdom that can only sustain a provost or a denier.
jokes.setup: Ben claims to have invented Cones of Dunshire. The Gryzzl employee calls him 'The Architect' sarcastically.
jokes.punchline: The employee jokes he's 'the alchemist of the Hinterlands,' and Ben immediately corrects this as a rules violation — proving his identity as the inventor by knowing details no one else would know.
jokes.explanation: A top-tier joke in the episode. Ben proving his identity as the game's inventor by immediately correcting an impossible role ('shadow kingdom that can only sustain a provost or a denier') is both absurdly funny AND a brilliant character moment. The detail is so specific and confident that it earns the laugh twice — once for the absurdity, once for the character reveal. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Winning is for people who are afraid of losing.

jokes.text: You wanna be corporal or warrior? / Neither. I'm the maverick.
jokes.setup: Ben challenges them to a game of Cones of Dunshire.
jokes.punchline: When offered existing roles, Ben declares himself 'the maverick' — a role that presumably doesn't exist in standard play, asserting creative authority as the inventor.
jokes.explanation: Ben establishing a special role for himself (the maverick) in his own game is a great beat. The confidence with which he asserts this unknown role — and the implication that as inventor he can do this — is perfect character logic.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? You're right. I'm gonna do this. I'm gonna open Ramsett's.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And you wanna know why? Because I'm tired of working for other people. I wanna work for myself. I wanna be my own boss.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Plus, I'm gonna make a ton of money and become super rich and famous.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then all the people who doubted me are gonna feel really stupid.

jokes.text: You know when it was completed? Last month.
jokes.setup: The official asks rhetorically when a merger from 2004 was completed — implying Leslie's timeline is dangerously optimistic.
jokes.punchline: 'Last month' — meaning 2014, a full decade after it started.
jokes.explanation: The delayed reveal — 'last month' for a 2004 merger — is perfectly structured. The economy of the punchline (two words) landing 10 years of bureaucratic failure is excellent. Good dark-bureaucratic humor.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's a great idea, Tom. I support you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Really? That means a lot coming from you, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Here's the bill for materials: $47,000. What a bargain.

jokes.text: I've been accused of a lot of things, but cavalier has never been one of them. I have a Super System.
jokes.setup: An official accuses Leslie of being cavalier about her town's future.
jokes.punchline: Leslie responds that she is definitively not cavalier — she has a 'Super System' — not realizing that the Super System is itself evidence of cavalier planning.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's self-seriousness as its own irony — the Super System as a rebuttal to accusations of poor planning is funny because it's the opposite of reassuring. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You just have to trust your instincts.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My instincts? Ben, my instincts told me to get bangs last year. I looked like a Afghan Hound for six months. My instincts also told me to marry Justin Long at a Dave & Buster's in Atlantic City. I can't trust my instincts! What if I make the wrong choice and I die alone in an airport taxi? Thirty years from now, I'm still in that taxi, riding in circles around O'Hare, and the driver doesn't even know I'm dead. He thinks I'm just being quiet. He turns up the radio a little bit. Now we're listening to John Tesh. I don't even like John Tesh!

jokes.text: You lost your cityhood?
jokes.setup: The official reveals his hometown 'was converted into unincorporated territory' — bureaucratic speak for a catastrophic civic failure.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's aghast 'You lost your cityhood?' — treating municipal status with the weight of a tragedy — is the reaction that sells the joke.
jokes.explanation: The phrasing 'lost your cityhood' as if it were a tangible possession or status is perfect Leslie Knope. Her horror at this scenario (unincorporated territory is her nightmare) reveals character while being funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you guys, do you realize this is where they filmed Star Wars? This is an actual Star Wars location!

jokes.text: That's a bold flavor. Fruity. A little earthy. / Which is it? Fruity or earthy? It can't be both, they're mutually exclusive!
jokes.setup: Donna and Craig are supposed to be working as a team wine tasting.
jokes.punchline: Craig immediately snaps at Donna's wine description — 'it can't be both, they're mutually exclusive!' — attacking the most basic, reasonable tasting note with absolute conviction.
jokes.explanation: Craig's unhinged certainty that fruity and earthy are mutually exclusive wine descriptors is a great character beat — his emotional volatility applied to oenology. The escalation to a near-breakdown over wine notes is very Craig.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love you! I mean, I love... the work that you're doing. For the Parks Department. I love that.

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: Oh, okay. Well, I appreciate that, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Great. So we're good?

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're good. Talk soon, Karen.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's Leslie.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. I don't know who I am anymore. A man without a palate isn't a man.
jokes.setup: Craig has just yelled at Donna about wine tasting.
jokes.punchline: He immediately collapses into an existential crisis — 'I don't know who I am anymore. A man without a palate isn't a man.'
jokes.explanation: The rapid escalation from anger to existential crisis is pure Craig comedy. 'A man without a palate isn't a man' as a philosophical statement applied to wine tasting is absurdly funny. The speed of his emotional arc is the joke.

jokes.text: I love you, Donna. / What are you guys doing? There's people waiting out there! / We're having a moment, you monster!
jokes.setup: Craig and Donna are having a genuine emotional moment about wine.
jokes.punchline: Tom interrupts what is clearly a personal breakthrough, and Craig calls him 'you monster' for disrupting it.
jokes.explanation: 'You monster!' directed at Tom for interrupting a wine-tasting emotional breakdown is very funny. The overblown response to a reasonable request is Craig in a nutshell. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Yo, yo, yo, yo, yo! What's up, fool? It's ya boy Jean-Ralphio, and I am back in the saddle, baby! Treat yo' self!

jokes.text: Ron, you're amazing. You've always been like a grandpa to me. But can you please lower your standards a tiny bit so my customers have somewhere to sit?
jokes.setup: Ron is rejecting chairs for being too perfect.
jokes.punchline: Tom sincerely compliments Ron (calls him a grandpa figure) then asks him to do worse work — a completely absurd request.
jokes.explanation: The inversion — asking someone to do worse work — is funny, and 'like a grandpa to me' is a sweet and specific compliment that makes the pivot to 'lower your standards' funnier. Good character interplay.

dialogue.speaker: Mona Lisa
dialogue.line: A group reservation? Oh, they're definitely trying to have group sex. Even in the morning, that's what it means.

jokes.text: Restaurant superstition, breaking a glass on the first night is good luck. / Thank God. [Larry immediately breaks another glass] Oh, geez. I'm so sorry. / Guess I have to start over. Who wants to go look for trees with me?
jokes.setup: Someone breaks a glass. Tom makes up a superstition to cover for it.
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately breaks another glass, and Ron's response to the catastrophe is to cheerfully announce he needs to go find more wood.
jokes.explanation: Three separate character beats work together: Tom's fast thinking (inventing superstition), Larry immediately destroying the cover story, and Ron's cheerful solution ('Who wants to go look for trees?'). Each beat is character-perfect, and the escalation structure is well-built.

dialogue.speaker: Mona Lisa
dialogue.line: Remember that time we tried to sell fake meds at the county fair?

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Oh yeah, that was tight!

dialogue.speaker: Mona Lisa
dialogue.line: Yeah, well it ended with me getting into a fistfight with a health inspector in the parking lot.

jokes.text: I play an action card to build a Belltower inside your Citadel. / My shaman casts a Toyber spell on your prosperity tile. / Looks like someone's out of resource gems.
jokes.setup: Ben is playing Cones of Dunshire against Gryzzl employees.
jokes.punchline: The game's terminology — 'Toyber spell,' 'prosperity tile,' 'resource gems' — spoken with complete seriousness by Silicon Valley tech bros in a competitive game context.
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of the game terminology spoken earnestly is funny, and the setting (competitive business negotiation via board game) is a good comedic premise. Less of a punchline and more of an extended absurdist moment.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: We should go to go-karts.

dialogue.speaker: Mona Lisa
dialogue.line: No, let's go to the hospital and watch them do autopsies.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Yeah, okay.

jokes.text: I move my abbot to the ocean hex, which moves my brinksman to the devil's lair, and pushes my farmer, yes, my humble farmer, directly into the central cone.
jokes.setup: Ben has been offered a draw while losing at Cones of Dunshire.
jokes.punchline: Ben's winning move is a preposterously complex chain of game mechanics culminating in his 'humble farmer' reaching the central cone — the dramatic pause on 'yes, my humble farmer' is perfect.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's funniest Cones of Dunshire moments. The combination of absurd game terminology, the dramatically escalating chain of mechanics, and the loving aside 'yes, my humble farmer' is excellent. The pause to honor the farmer is the perfect comedic beat. Deeply Ben Wyatt.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The volunteer group name is way too long.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? You're right. We should get smaller hats.

jokes.text: Yeah, man! We did it! This whole company is ours! / Oh, no, it's not. That's mine. That's mine. It's all mine.
jokes.setup: Ben wins the Cones of Dunshire game, earning another shot at the WiFi pitch.
jokes.punchline: Andy celebrates as if they won everything — 'This whole company is ours!' — and Ben immediately and firmly corrects him on the intellectual property.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Andy/Ben dynamic — Andy's overreach met with Ben's precision. 'That's mine. It's all mine.' delivered with such firmness is a good beat. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: "She made Pawnee better." Ironic, given that she's leaving.

jokes.text: Spaghetti, linguine, fettuccine, ravioli, rigatoni, Ferrari, Lamborghini, bucatini, lasagna.
jokes.setup: April is reciting the menu from memory when a customer asks her to repeat it.
jokes.punchline: On the second recitation, she slips in 'Ferrari' and 'Lamborghini' between the pasta names — which the customer apparently doesn't notice.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. April's list is so rhythmically similar to the real pasta names that the customer (and audience on first pass) might not catch 'Ferrari' and 'Lamborghini.' The fact that she doesn't flinch, and the customer apparently accepts it, is perfectly April — minimal effort, maximum subversion. The structure is flawless and it's highly quotable. Strong candidate for standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Colin Meloy
dialogue.line: Pawnee is amazing. We've been all over the world, and I've never seen a town like this.

dialogue.speaker: Chris Krosby
dialogue.line: What do you mean?

dialogue.speaker: Colin Meloy
dialogue.line: Well, for starters, we went to this restaurant called JJ's Diner, and they have a thing called a 'Sweetums Burger.' It's a burger stuffed with candy, marshmallows, and whipped cream.

dialogue.speaker: Nate Query
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Colin Meloy
dialogue.line: And then we went to this other place, and they told us the local specialty is a hot dog wrapped in a cinnamon roll, served with a side of chocolate gravy.

jokes.text: We had to throw our menus away because they are covered with pictures of Larry's dog's rectum.
jokes.setup: A customer asks to see a menu.
jokes.punchline: April delivers the explanation for the missing menus completely straight — the dog rectum fact stated as flat business information.
jokes.explanation: The callback pays off beautifully — the explanation delivered with April's complete deadpan is funnier than the original setup. 'Covered with pictures of Larry's dog's rectum' spoken to a customer as if it's a normal explanation is excellent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I been on house arrest so many times, they're gonna use my case in law school. They're calling it 'The State v. Jean-Ralphio: A Study in Repeat Offenses.'

jokes.text: Great news. Lord Sheldon's gonna make it. Yeah. We just have to apply a salve to his anus every hour for the rest of his life, but... Oh! Enjoy your meal!
jokes.setup: Larry comes out with good news about his dog while customers are at the table.
jokes.punchline: The good news involves hourly salve application to the dog's anus — delivered at a restaurant table before a chipper 'Enjoy your meal!'
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the dog rectum running gag — now applied anus salve is described in graphic detail at the restaurant table, capped with 'Enjoy your meal!' — is structurally excellent. Larry's complete inability to read the room is perfect character comedy. The timing of 'Enjoy your meal!' is the key.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: My case is so unprecedented, law schools use it on their exams. Professor's like, 'Here's Jean-Ralphio Saperstein. What would you do?' And the answer is always 'The opposite of that.'

jokes.text: People are playing with my cones, babe.
jokes.setup: Ben discovers Cones of Dunshire has spread virally across the internet.
jokes.punchline: His summary: 'People are playing with my cones, babe.' The unintentional double entendre and complete earnestness makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The phrase is funny both for its earnestness and its unintentional suggestiveness. Ben is entirely sincere, which makes it work. Economy is excellent — the whole joy of the Cones of Dunshire arc compressed into one line.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I will embarrass you with childhood stories.

dialogue.speaker: Ginuwine
dialogue.line: You wouldn't dare.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Oh really? Remember your rubber duckies? You called them the Quack-son 5.

dialogue.speaker: Ginuwine
dialogue.line: Donna, no...

jokes.text: I mean, how far along are we on human cloning? Wasn't Dolly the sheep like 20 years ago? It's like, 'What the hell, scientists? Get it together!'
jokes.setup: Leslie is wrestling with whether she can both leave Pawnee and stay.
jokes.punchline: Her proposed solution is human cloning, and her frustration at scientists for not solving this yet is delivered as a genuine complaint.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's solution to an impossible decision being 'human cloning' is very on-brand. The specific reference to Dolly and the frustrated 'What the hell, scientists? Get it together!' is a great detail. Her earnestness about scientific progress as a personal disappointment is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy Two
dialogue.line: I'm here looking for fathers. Single fathers, preferably. I'm not here to engage in any kind of ritual sacrifice or anything like that.

jokes.text: We are not going back to Pawnee until we know we are staying in Pawnee.
jokes.setup: Ben says they're going to miss their flight; Leslie refuses to leave the cab.
jokes.punchline: The logical paradox of Leslie's ultimatum — 'not going back until we know we're staying' — reveals her circular anxiety.
jokes.explanation: The paradox is the joke — Leslie's 'decision paralysis expressed as a definitive statement' is a good character beat. Well-structured but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: I'm going to defeat you, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: How?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: By seducing you.

jokes.text: Really? I love quitting. When I was a kid and things didn't go my way, I would just take my ball and go home. That's better than winning, 'cause then, your friends can't play anymore!
jokes.setup: Ron says 'It is my belief that you never start a job you don't intend to finish.'
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately advocates for quitting as superior to finishing — his childhood philosophy was explicitly designed to deny his friends the ability to play.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom character comedy. The revelation that his childhood quitting strategy was deliberately anti-social ('then your friends can't play anymore') is darkly funny and completely in character. The cheerful delivery of what is essentially a selfish manifesto is very Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: If you try to leave me, Ron, I will destroy you. I will take everything you have.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: You know what? Bring it on. I've defeated every challenge life has thrown at me. Taxes, bureaucrats, people who talk during movies... I'm not afraid of you.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Oh Ron, when I'm done with you, you won't know what hit you. I'm going to make you surrender in the most intimate way possible.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: ...Is this going somewhere?

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Oh yes, it is.

jokes.text: Well, I hate doing work, but I love being flattered, so maybe I'll give it another try.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been laying compliments on Tom to get him to reopen the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Tom lays out his decision-making process with complete transparency — flattery beats his work aversion.
jokes.explanation: A classic Tom Haverford line — perfectly self-aware, perfectly economical. 'I hate doing work, but I love being flattered' is a great character summary in one sentence. The 'so maybe I'll give it another try' as the logical conclusion is excellent. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, why are you so excited about being Larry? He's literally the worst character.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't know, I think Larry's kind of endearing in his own way.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'm opening a restaurant and it's going to be so incredible that people will forget all about this show. Actually, they'll forget about everything. My restaurant will be the only thing that matters to anyone ever.

jokes.text: Because you currently owe me $16,000. For the wood. The labor was free, but the wood was a bargain. At $16,000.
jokes.setup: Ron tells Tom this is a 'smart move' — and Tom thanks him.
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately reveals his friendship speech was a preamble to a $16,000 bill — and describes this price as 'a bargain.'
jokes.explanation: Ron's pivot from encouragement to bill-collection is a great character beat. 'The labor was free, but the wood was a bargain. At $16,000.' — the placement of 'At $16,000' after 'bargain' is structurally perfect. Very Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Only Larry wants to come to Chicago with us?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, what's wrong with that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What's wrong with that?!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I mean, Larry's great. He's reliable, he's honest...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, everyone hates Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: They do?

jokes.text: I'm never gonna be able to decide. I'm gonna be paralyzed by hypotheticals until I die here, in this minivan! At the San Francisco airport.
jokes.setup: Leslie is stuck in a cab trying to make a decision.
jokes.punchline: Her catastrophizing peaks at dying in the cab — then she adds the mundane geographical detail 'At the San Francisco airport,' as if that's the real tragedy.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from hypotheticals to dying in a minivan is funny, and the kicker 'At the San Francisco airport' grounds the absurdity with specificity. The precision of the location as a final indignity is a good touch.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I'll have your signature cocktail.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: That's a combination of vodka, cranberry juice, and oxycodone.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: Perfect. I'm in a lot of pain.

jokes.text: Wait. I'm on Endor. / These are the redwoods George Lucas used to create the forest moon of Endor. / Sorry, that's not why we're here. Let's go.
jokes.setup: Ben brings Leslie to the redwoods in Muir Woods for an important emotional moment.
jokes.punchline: Ben's first response to the majestic redwoods is to identify them as the Star Wars filming location — and then immediately corrects himself and moves on.
jokes.explanation: Deeply Ben Wyatt — his nerd credentials showing at an emotionally important moment, then his own self-awareness kicking in ('Sorry, that's not why we're here'). The beat is structurally perfect and highly character-integrated. His inability to fully suppress the Star Wars reference is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Jeremy, your hair is so curly. I wonder if the carpet matches the drapes.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy
dialogue.line: Tammy, that's inappropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy
dialogue.line: Oh please, everyone wonders.

jokes.text: Hi, Grant. I want the job. Uh, I have a lot of questions, but I'm a little amped up right now, so I'll probably just hang up. Might be for the best. But anyway, I love you. No, I don't. I'm sorry. That was weird. Okay, bye.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just decided to take the job and immediately calls Grant.
jokes.punchline: Her call collapses from professional opener to 'I love you' to immediate retraction to 'that was weird' to hanging up — a rapid descent into social chaos.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best comedic moments. The rapid escalation from professional to awkward to 'I love you' to retraction to apology to hanging up is structurally excellent — each step is funnier than the last. 'No, I don't. I'm sorry. That was weird. Okay, bye.' is a perfect comedic sequence. Amy Poehler would deliver this brilliantly. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We should get divorced just so we can get married again.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I love that idea.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right? We could do it next weekend.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm already looking up lawyers.

jokes.text: This is Lester Kanopf. / No, you know... Okay. Bye. / Smoothly handled, Lester. / Yeah. I panicked.
jokes.setup: After Leslie's chaotic phone call, Grant apparently makes a similarly awkward one and introduces himself as 'Lester Kanopf.'
jokes.punchline: The callback to the opening check-in name error — Grant calls himself 'Lester Kanopf' and Leslie deadpans 'Smoothly handled, Lester.' Grant's 'Yeah. I panicked.' is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the 'Lester Kanopf' name from the opening works beautifully — it's earned, it recontextualizes the earlier joke, and 'Yeah. I panicked.' is a great self-aware line. Good economy and structural payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm gonna take a 'You-ie.' That's a photo of you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's the opposite of a selfie.

jokes.text: I've decided to start with Larry. As a practice run. Because it doesn't need to go well. Because, who cares? Because, Larry.
jokes.setup: Leslie needs to tell her staff she's leaving and wants to work up to it.
jokes.punchline: She starts with Larry specifically because his reaction doesn't matter — 'because, who cares? Because, Larry.' — the dismissiveness of 'Because, Larry' as a complete argument.
jokes.explanation: A sharp Larry joke that both participates in the show's Larry-dismissal running gag and subverts it slightly by showing Leslie's fondness even in her cruelty. 'Because, Larry.' as a self-sufficient argument is extremely quotable. Dark but characteristically warm in the P&R way.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: They deserve each other. Within six months, they'll either be married or one of them will be dead.

jokes.text: She wanted to fire me, but she realized that she loved having me around too much, and she couldn't do it.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just been trying to tell Larry she's leaving for a new job — not firing him.
jokes.punchline: Larry completely misreads the scene and tells colleagues he was almost fired but Leslie loves him too much — an entirely fabricated narrative.
jokes.explanation: Larry's obliviousness creating a completely false positive story is a great character beat. The gap between what happened (she couldn't say she was leaving) and Larry's interpretation (she loves him too much to fire him) is funny and character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you've been secretly performing as a smooth jazz saxophonist this whole time?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's not something I advertise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not advertise? Ron, you've been lying to me! To all of us! How could you—wait, that solo on 'Midnight in Pawnee' was YOU?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ron, that was beautiful. I'm not even mad anymore. Actually, I'm deeply moved. But here's what's going to happen: you're going to perform at the Harvest Festival, you're going to let me document it for the Parks Department social media, and you're going to smile—just a little—while you do it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: ...We'll discuss it.

jokes.text: Why didn't you fire Larry? I thought you were going to fire him.
jokes.setup: Leslie returns from her Larry conversation without having told him anything.
jokes.punchline: Her colleagues are disappointed she didn't fire Larry — they had been waiting for this.
jokes.explanation: A functional extension of the Larry running gag. The colleagues' disappointment at his continued employment is on-brand for the show. Reliable but not a standout.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, Ron played saxophone? Ron, you're a man of so many hidden talents.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't think of it as hidden. I simply don't discuss my personal affairs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, you were incredible. I had no idea you could play like that. Ron, you have to teach me. Please. I'm begging you.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Because you're loud and you don't listen, and those are the two worst qualities in a student of the saxophone.

jokes.text: Did someone call for a party zoo?
jokes.setup: Tom announces he's called in reinforcements for the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio enters announcing himself as a 'party zoo' — his self-branding is typically delusional and over-the-top.
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's entrance line is perfectly in character. 'Party zoo' as self-description is the ideal amount of absurd confidence. His very presence raises the comic energy of any scene.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're a federal employee, right? So you can revive canceled TV shows?

jokes.text: All right, so we got a four-way going with my ex, my brother, and this rando? Okay, if that's where the night is going. / It's 9:00 in the morning.
jokes.setup: Tom introduces Jean-Ralphio and Mona Lisa to Craig.
jokes.punchline: Mona Lisa misreads the business arrangement as a sexual invitation and immediately accepts, requiring Tom to correct her — and Craig noting the time.
jokes.explanation: Mona Lisa's complete misinterpretation is very in character. Craig's '9:00 in the morning' as the correction rather than moral objection is a funny choice. Good character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ed, you're fired. You're incompetent and you're lazy.

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: Terry agrees.

jokes.text: I stole $2,000 from you. I'm the person that sneaks into your home every night, and eats your food. Oh, so... Oh, right, so I do owe you a favor.
jokes.setup: Tom argues Jean-Ralphio owes him a favor.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's counter-argument — listing his own crimes against Tom — inadvertently convinces himself that he does owe Tom a favor. The logic is completely inverted.
jokes.explanation: A structurally excellent joke. Jean-Ralphio argues against owing Tom a favor, lists his own crimes (theft, breaking and entering, eating his food), and this somehow convinces him he DOES owe a favor. The inverted logic resolving in agreement is brilliant character comedy. 'I'm the person that sneaks into your home every night and eats your food' is also a standalone great line.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ed, I'm going to have to let you go. You lost those files and that's just unacceptable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And Terry, your coffee order is always wrong anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But Ed, back to you — you're fired.

jokes.text: You remember the time you made me dress up as you, and go on a date with one of your ex-boyfriends? And then the guy immediately figured it out, and beat me up? / Oh... / Now you remember that I got beat up.
jokes.setup: Mona Lisa argues Tom owes her a favor.
jokes.punchline: The story — Tom made her impersonate him on a date, the guy immediately saw through it and beat her up — is absurd enough, but the kicker 'Now you remember that I got beat up' (implying Tom had forgotten) makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: The absurd backstory is funny on its own, but 'Now you remember that I got beat up' is the perfect kicker — implying Tom had completely forgotten this incident in which she was physically assaulted on his behalf. Dark, absurd, and character-specific.

jokes.text: Thank you, Andrew. But fun or not, playing music is something I like to keep private, along with my family, my conversations, and my whereabouts at all times.
jokes.setup: Andy invites Ron to perform at the Unity Concert as Duke Silver.
jokes.punchline: Ron declines, listing what he keeps private — and 'my whereabouts at all times' being on this list is a darkly funny statement of his paranoid self-sufficiency.
jokes.explanation: A great Ron Swanson character joke. The list escalates from reasonable (music, family) to understandable (conversations) to revealing (whereabouts at all times). The last item perfectly encapsulates Ron's extreme privacy as a lifestyle philosophy. Highly character-integrated and quotable.

jokes.text: Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to accept the following missions.
jokes.setup: Andy begins his team briefing using Mission: Impossible language.
jokes.punchline: The Mission: Impossible phrase is completed with tautological nonsense — 'is to accept the following missions' — the movie trope eaten by itself.
jokes.explanation: Andy's pop culture reference eaten by his own obliviousness — he uses the setup but can't complete it meaningfully. 'Should you choose to accept it... is to accept the following missions' is a clean self-referential loop. Very Andy.

jokes.text: Larry. Staying out of the way.
jokes.setup: Andy is assigning tasks to everyone at the planning meeting.
jokes.punchline: Larry's assignment is 'staying out of the way' — not a task but a prohibition.
jokes.explanation: A reliable Larry running gag executed with excellent economy. Three words conveying a complete character relationship. Not original but perfectly delivered.

jokes.text: Your main goal today is to get 2,000 people to sign up for the Pawnee-Eagleton Merger Preservation Volunteer Action Squad. / Their first project will be to come up with a shorter name for the group.
jokes.setup: Andy announces the goal and the name of the volunteer squad.
jokes.punchline: He immediately acknowledges the name is terrible and that coming up with a better one is their first task.
jokes.explanation: A solid setup/punchline — announce absurdly long name, immediately acknowledge the problem. The joke is in the timing of the self-correction. Functional and well-structured.

jokes.text: You're right, the name is too long, I was picturing bigger hats.
jokes.setup: Andy says the group name is too long and their first project is shortening it.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's only objection to the long name was that she envisioned bigger hats — suggesting she was fully committed to the name if the hats could be bigger.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'I was picturing bigger hats' is completely inexplicable and perfect. The logic that the long name = bigger hats = acceptable is pure Leslie Knope absurdist planning. Maximum economy, deeply character-specific. Highly quotable and a strong candidate for standout moment.

jokes.text: The story of these nuts is... they're mixed.
jokes.setup: Craig is pitching to someone at the Unity Concert, apparently about snacks.
jokes.punchline: His entire 'story' for the mixed nuts is: they're mixed. The dramatic setup ('The story of these nuts is...') deflates to the most basic description.
jokes.explanation: A tiny gem of a joke. The dramatic wind-up ('The story of these nuts is...') punctured by 'they're mixed' is a perfect anti-climax. Craig's pitch collapses into tautology. Excellent economy.

jokes.text: Well, will there be music, food... And a location? / Yes. / Good, because in this reporter's opinion, it's not a party unless there's music, food, and a location.
jokes.setup: Craig is inviting a celebrity reporter to the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Perd Hapley's party-evaluation criteria include 'a location' as a distinct requirement — and he confirms this is the standard he operates by as a reporter.
jokes.explanation: Pure Perd Hapley — his 'reporter' framing of opinions, and the tautological inclusion of 'a location' as a party requirement, is perfectly in character. 'In this reporter's opinion' as a shield for mundane statements is a great Perd beat.

jokes.text: It's not that great. Doesn't even look like you. Or actually, you know what? It kinda does.
jokes.setup: Leslie is crying over the statue; someone tries to comfort her.
jokes.punchline: The comfort attempt — 'it's not that great' — pivots to 'doesn't even look like you,' then immediately reverses to 'it kinda does' — a failed attempt at a compliment that accidentally confirms she looks like a government statue.
jokes.explanation: A functional comedy beat. The back-and-forth correction is a common comedic structure but the pivot from consolation to accidental insult ('it kinda does look like you') lands.

jokes.text: Hello, Pawnee, we're The Decemberists. / It's great to be here. This is truly an amazing town. I ordered a small cheeseburger and both the buns were pizzas.
jokes.setup: The Decemberists take the stage at the Unity Concert.
jokes.punchline: Their endorsement of Pawnee peaks at 'both the buns were pizzas' — a genuinely absurd food observation that serves as the highest praise they can give.
jokes.explanation: A great Pawnee worldbuilding joke delivered by an actual celebrity band. 'Both the buns were pizzas' as a sincere endorsement of the town plays on Pawnee's established food-excess mythology. The specificity and the genuine delight implied make it very funny. The real band's commitment sells it.

jokes.text: Victoria Secret supermodel Karlie Kloss? Really? Where? / Wait a second. You're not Karlie, you're my friend, Joan Callamezzo. / They don't even allow me in Victoria's Secret anymore. / Why? / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio appears to spot a celebrity.
jokes.punchline: It's just Joan Callamezzo — whom he knows — and her response to the Victoria's Secret mention is to note she's banned from the store. The 'Why?' / 'Yeah.' exchange is a perfect non-answer.
jokes.explanation: The 'Why?' / 'Yeah.' beat at the end is perfect — Joan doesn't answer, Jean-Ralphio accepts this. The implication that the answer would be too complicated (or shameful) is funnier than any explanation. Good economy in the exchange.

jokes.text: The only reason I wouldn't be there is if I got pulled over. For violating my house arrest.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is confirming he'll come to the restaurant party.
jokes.punchline: His only potential obstacle is house arrest violation — mentioned as casually as traffic.
jokes.explanation: Very Jean-Ralphio — his legal troubles mentioned as minor logistical concerns. The casualness is the joke. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Judge gave me two ankle bracelets. Said it was the first time he ever had to do that. Ja boy's a question on the bar exam! Ya heard!
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is revealing his legal situation.
jokes.punchline: He has TWO ankle bracelets (unprecedented), and his pride at being a law school exam question is completely unironic.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from house arrest to two ankle bracelets (an unprecedented sentence) to being a bar exam question — and Jean-Ralphio's unhinged PRIDE in all of this — is excellent. 'Ja boy's a question on the bar exam!' is a very quotable line delivered with the perfect amount of misplaced joy.

jokes.text: You ever heard of Warrant? / Yeah. / There's a cover band right here, that call themselves Cherry Pie. Pretty sure we got their bass player.
jokes.setup: Jamm is trying to pitch his secession rally as a better event than the Unity Concert.
jokes.punchline: His big draw is a Warrant cover band, and he hedges even that: 'Pretty sure we got their bass player.'
jokes.explanation: Jamm's underqualified pitch — a cover band, and maybe only the bass player — is a good deflation joke. The hedge 'pretty sure' perfectly calibrates how little he actually has. Good economy.

jokes.text: Ginuwine, it is an honor to be breathing the same air as you. No joke. But real talk, we're both men about town being constantly bombarded with party invitations.
jokes.setup: Donna is approaching Ginuwine (the real R&B singer) to invite him to the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Donna opens with extreme deference ('no joke') but immediately pivots to establishing equivalence — she and Ginuwine are both 'men about town' facing the same 'bombardment' of invitations.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from reverence to peer-framing is very Donna. 'We're both men about town' is particularly funny given Donna is a woman. Her confidence in establishing this equivalence with an actual celebrity is excellent character comedy.

jokes.text: Unless you want me to get on stage and talk about how we used to take baths together. How you cried whenever I took away your rubber duckies. / Damn, Donna, why you gotta bring the Quackson Five into this?
jokes.setup: Donna is leveraging a personal relationship with Ginuwine to get him to the party.
jokes.punchline: Ginuwine's nickname for his childhood rubber ducks — 'the Quackson Five' — is revealed as his response to the bath/rubber duck story.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's single best jokes. 'The Quackson Five' is an inspired piece of writing — the Jackson Five pun applied to rubber ducks, revealed as a childhood name Ginuwine actually used, and then delivered with 'why you gotta bring the Quackson Five into this?' as if this is sensitive history. The specificity, the wordplay, the indignation — all perfect. Highly quotable, strong rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Imaginary friends are cool / Imaginary friends take the fall for you
jokes.setup: Andy/Johnny Karate is performing for children at the Unity Concert.
jokes.punchline: A children's song lyric that endorses blaming imaginary friends for your mistakes — dark subversive content packaged as kids' entertainment.
jokes.explanation: A dark little gem — 'imaginary friends take the fall for you' as wholesome children's content is subversive. Andy writing a song that teaches kids to scapegoat their imaginary friends is very on-brand.

jokes.text: Preparing a ritual sacrifice of a newborn? / No, just trolling for some daddy. Sorry, I pronounced that wrong. I'm trolling for some dad-dy.
jokes.setup: Ron asks Tammy what she's doing at a children's performance.
jokes.punchline: Tammy's response ('trolling for some daddy') initially sounds crude, then she 'corrects' herself to 'dad-dy' — which is also crude but in a different way. The fake self-correction is the joke.
jokes.explanation: An excellent Tammy joke. The fake correction ('I pronounced that wrong') pretends to fix a crude statement by replacing it with another crude statement. The structure is deceptively smart — the 'correction' is the punchline. Very Tammy, who weaponizes sexuality at all times.

jokes.text: Diane, why don't you take the girls for some ice cream while I dispose of this sewer-dwelling gutter witch?
jokes.setup: Tammy has appeared and Ron needs to deal with her without upsetting his family.
jokes.punchline: 'While I dispose of this sewer-dwelling gutter witch' — spoken as casually as 'while I take a phone call.'
jokes.explanation: 'Sewer-dwelling gutter witch' as a casual description of his ex-wife — delivered as parenthetically as possible — is excellent Ron. The juxtaposition of the polite family request ('take the girls for ice cream') and the colorful insult is very strong. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: I will defeat you right into my pants.
jokes.setup: Tammy is trying to convince Ron she will win him back.
jokes.punchline: 'I will defeat you right into my pants' — mixing competitive and sexual language in a way that is uniquely Tammy.
jokes.explanation: An exceptional line. 'I will defeat you right into my pants' is a perfect Tammy line — it merges combat metaphors with sexual ones in a way that makes complete sense for her character while being completely outrageous. Maximum economy (7 words), deeply character-specific, extremely quotable. One of the episode's standout moments.

jokes.text: I always figured we'd break up because I got drafted by the Colts. And then in the first game, of course, I break my leg. The crowd starts chanting my name, and I give them the thumbs up. And then I go to the hospital, I get really good at chess, I end up beating the computer finally. And then the band just sort of drifts apart. That was how I saw it.
jokes.setup: Andy is apologizing to a former bandmate about how Mouse Rat broke up.
jokes.punchline: Andy has an elaborate, extremely specific fantasy about how the band was supposed to break up — including being drafted by the Colts, breaking his leg heroically, getting good at chess, and THEN the band drifting. Every element escalates the absurdity.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's very best jokes. Andy's alternate-history fantasy is perfectly structured — each element (NFL draft, heroic injury, chess championship, THEN band drift) builds on the last with escalating absurdity and complete sincerity. 'The crowd starts chanting my name, and I give them the thumbs up' as a specific detail in what is already a fantasy is inspired. The ending 'that was how I saw it, but...' is a perfect deflation. Deep character integration — only Andy Dwyer would have worked out this exact narrative.

jokes.text: One kid peed his pants because he didn't want to miss anything. / What? / I gave a kid pee-pants? / Yes! / That's why I do what I do.
jokes.setup: April is reporting on Andy's performance success.
jokes.punchline: The metric for success is a child urinating themselves rather than leave — and Andy's emotional response ('That's why I do what I do') treats this as the highest artistic compliment.
jokes.explanation: A great joke. 'I gave a kid pee-pants' as a moment of artistic pride is genuinely funny and completely on-brand for Andy. The structure — April's casual delivery, Andy's dawning realization, then the full emotional commitment — is well-built. 'That's why I do what I do' as a sincere artistic statement about pee-pants is the perfect punchline.

jokes.text: I hope you like deep-dish pizza, because there's gonna be a lot more of it in Chicago, where we're all gonna be moving.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to persuade her friends to move with her.
jokes.punchline: She pre-announces that everyone is moving as if it's settled — using pizza as the lure — before anyone has agreed.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's assumption that everyone will follow her is character-appropriate, and using pizza as the argument is funny, but this is a softer joke that serves plot more than comedy.

jokes.text: Pawnee is cheap and we like it here, and Chicago seems like there's a lot of stuff to do and people, but I like to do nothing with no one. So, thank you and I love you, but no thank you, and I hate you. More I love you.
jokes.setup: Leslie is pitching everyone on moving to Chicago.
jokes.punchline: April's rejection is a perfectly April statement that starts with reasonable objections and collapses into emotional contradiction: 'thank you and I love you, but no thank you, and I hate you. More I love you.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. April's rejection is both perfectly character-captured ('I like to do nothing with no one') and structurally brilliant — the emotional reversal from love to hate back to 'more I love you' is a beautiful absurdist sequence. 'I like to do nothing with no one' is extremely quotable as a statement of personal philosophy.

jokes.text: Thank you, Pawnee! We have been Bobby Knight Ranger!
jokes.setup: A band finishes their set at the Unity Concert.
jokes.punchline: The band name 'Bobby Knight Ranger' — a fusion of Indiana basketball coach Bobby Knight and the band Night Ranger.
jokes.explanation: A solid Pawnee-specific pun — Bobby Knight (Indiana's legendary/controversial basketball coach) merged with Night Ranger. The specificity to Indiana culture makes it earn its place. Good economy.

jokes.text: Thursday night we're opening for Steely Dan Quayle!
jokes.setup: Band is wrapping up their set.
jokes.punchline: Steely Dan Quayle — fusing the band Steely Dan with former VP Dan Quayle — as a band name reveal.
jokes.explanation: A second political-band name pun — Steely Dan Quayle works better as a word construction than Bobby Knight Ranger because it's a more natural-sounding name. The Indiana/political specificity of the show is well-served by this.
