jokes.text: Super cool to hear Sister Christian that many times in a row!
jokes.setup: A Night Ranger cover band has apparently been playing 'Sister Christian' on repeat.
jokes.punchline: Andy's deadpan 'Super cool to hear Sister Christian that many times in a row' — the politeness cannot conceal the implication that this was too many.
jokes.explanation: Andy's forced positivity about a clearly bad situation is a reliable comic engine. The implication that Sister Christian was played several times in a row is funnier because it's never stated outright.

jokes.text: I don't know, it sounds pretty good to me. The windy city, me, my lady, my boy Lar-bones...
jokes.setup: Leslie is horrified that only Larry wants to join them in Chicago.
jokes.punchline: Ben seems genuinely fine with 'Larry and no one' as a scenario, warmly referring to Larry as 'my boy Lar-bones' — either sincerely or to tease Leslie.
jokes.explanation: A nice character beat. 'My boy Lar-bones' is an affectionate nickname that lands perfectly, and Ben's equanimity about Larry is a sweet contrast to Leslie's horror. Works as a button on the previous joke.

jokes.text: I once got into a cab that Kyra Sedgwick was getting out of! / No way, the closer?
jokes.setup: The team is told this is the most important night of Tom's life.
jokes.punchline: Craig's competing claim for a personally important night is sharing a cab transition with Kyra Sedgwick — not meeting her, not speaking to her, just entering a cab she was exiting.
jokes.explanation: A strong Craig character joke. The specificity of Kyra Sedgwick (mid-tier celebrity) and the near-total non-interaction (she was getting out as he was getting in) as Craig's pinnacle celebrity encounter is very funny. 'No way, the closer?' as the response — genuinely confirming the celebrity reference — is a nice extra beat.

jokes.text: Can you squeeze me in, or do I need a reservation? 'Cause there's nobody here.
jokes.setup: Saperstein comes to the restaurant pretending it could possibly be full.
jokes.punchline: He asks for a reservation while openly noting the restaurant is empty — the politeness of the question making the insult more pointed.
jokes.explanation: Saperstein's particular cruelty — the polite form of humiliation — is well-executed. The simultaneity of asking for a reservation while noting the emptiness is good comic structure.

jokes.text: I'll have the 'Joan.' It's a tumbler of gin and it's got crushed aspirin around the rim. / And I would just like an empty glass.
jokes.setup: Joan and Perd are ordering drinks at Tom's Bistro.
jokes.punchline: Joan's cocktail is a gin tumbler with crushed aspirin on the rim (a hangover drink for people who never stopped), and Perd orders an empty glass.
jokes.explanation: Two excellent character jokes stacked. Joan's signature cocktail — 'crushed aspirin around the rim' — is a perfect distillation of her character (a hard-drinking local TV personality). Perd ordering 'an empty glass' is completely inexplicable and perfect Perd — he has a reason for it that we don't need to hear. Both drinks tell us everything about the characters in one order. Highly quotable and deeply character-integrated.

jokes.text: Yeah, sure, man, you got it, no problem. I mean, dudes gotta stick together, right? Right? Man, she is wearing that dress, though. Oh! Mmm.
jokes.setup: Ron asks Jamm not to sleep with Tammy, calling on bro solidarity.
jokes.punchline: Jamm immediately agrees, asks for confirmation, then within seconds is overtaken by Tammy's attractiveness — the solidarity dissolving in real time.
jokes.explanation: Jamm's commitment to bro code evaporating instantly is a reliable character beat. The 'Mmm' at the end as capitulation is a good economy moment. Not exceptional but well-executed.

jokes.text: Promise me you won't sleep with her, even though it would be quite easy, and certainly mind-blowing.
jokes.setup: Ron explains to Jamm that Tammy is nearby and sexually voracious, asking Jamm not to sleep with her.
jokes.punchline: Ron's plea includes acknowledgment that sleeping with Tammy would be 'quite easy' and 'certainly mind-blowing' — a begrudging tribute to his ex-wife's sexual prowess embedded in his desperate request.
jokes.explanation: A great Ron/Tammy joke. The dark comedy is in Ron's uncontrollable honesty — he can't even make a simple request without accidentally endorsing Tammy's appeal. 'Quite easy, and certainly mind-blowing' reads as Ron's own first-hand assessment. The self-undermining quality is very Ron.

jokes.text: Hi, Ben! It's me, Barney, from the accounting firm. Yes, hi, Barney. You don't have to introduce yourself every time.
jokes.setup: A recurring accountant character greets Ben.
jokes.punchline: Ben establishes that Barney introduces himself every time they meet — a simple but funny character quirk.
jokes.explanation: A simple but functional character bit. The 'you don't have to introduce yourself every time' establishes a running gag in one line. Economy is good. Not a standout but does its job.

jokes.text: This is amazing. How can I ever repay you? / Come work for us at the accounting firm? / Okay. / No, sorry, I can't. / Wow. Shortest one yet.
jokes.setup: Barney gives Ben the Cones of Dunshire copyright, and Ben asks how to repay him.
jokes.punchline: Ben agrees to the accounting job offer immediately, then immediately rescinds it — and Barney notes this is 'the shortest one yet,' implying this exact pattern has happened before.
jokes.explanation: Excellent setup/punchline with a great escalation. 'Wow. Shortest one yet.' implies a whole history of Ben briefly agreeing to things then immediately backing out — characterizing both his impulsiveness and his tendency to please before reconsidering. The delivery of 'Okay. / No, sorry, I can't.' with minimal space is the key.

jokes.text: I wonder if the carpet is as curly as the drapes.
jokes.setup: Tammy spots Jeremy Jamm and becomes interested in him.
jokes.punchline: Her assessment of Jamm is delivered as a classic euphemism for body hair — an extremely crude observation made with complete Tammy nonchalance.
jokes.explanation: A classic Tammy crude observation. The visual euphemism applied to Jamm (who has notoriously curly hair) is character-perfect. High character integration — only Tammy would say this at a public event.

jokes.text: Babe, thank you so much for organizing the Mouse Rat reunion. / It was actually Ginuwine who arranged everything. He really cares about you.
jokes.setup: Andy thanks April for the Mouse Rat reunion.
jokes.punchline: April reveals it was actually Ginuwine — the R&B singer — who organized it out of genuine care for Andy. The absurdity of a celebrity doing this as a personal favor is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Ginuwine cares about Andy and organized his reunion is sweetly absurd. It pays off the Donna/Ginuwine relationship established earlier and adds a layer to Andy's character. Functional.

jokes.text: Let's get divorced. That way we can get married again! / Yes! Let's do it. You want to? / Yes! / We should do that, right? / Yeah, totally. / We're getting divorced! / Yes!
jokes.setup: Andy says he wishes he could marry April all over again.
jokes.punchline: April suggests they get divorced specifically so they can get married again — and both of them are immediately and fully committed to this plan.
jokes.explanation: A great April and Andy moment. The logic (divorce = opportunity to remarry) is absurd but makes complete sense for these characters, and their mutual escalating commitment ('We're getting divorced! Yes!') is perfect. The joy with which they embrace an unnecessary divorce is deeply them.

jokes.text: Except for Liam Hemsworth and Miley Cyrus. I was hoping tonight would be magical enough to get them back together. / Let it go, friend. He's not good enough for her. / And vice-versa!
jokes.setup: Tom is counting his celebrity guests at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals he was trying to use the party to reunite Liam Hemsworth and Miley Cyrus (who had recently split). Ben and Leslie's differing opinions — 'He's not good enough for her' / 'And vice-versa!' — as a rapid exchange.
jokes.explanation: The celebrity gossip angle is somewhat topical (the Hemsworth/Cyrus split was recent), and the exchange between Ben and Leslie covering both sides is a quick and functional joke. Not deeply character-specific but gets the job done.

jokes.text: I just had the best Italian meal I've ever had in my life. And I've been to Dallas.
jokes.setup: Saperstein is admitting Tom's Bistro is excellent.
jokes.punchline: 'And I've been to Dallas' — using Dallas as the pinnacle of Italian food sophistication, which is itself the joke.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Dallas as the Italian food reference point is the joke — not Rome, not New York, not even Chicago, but Dallas. It reveals Saperstein's frame of reference while being genuinely funny. Excellent economy — 'And I've been to Dallas' does everything.

jokes.text: Do you mind if I snap a 'You-ie'? / It's what I call selfies of other people.
jokes.setup: Tom wants a photo with Kay Hanley.
jokes.punchline: Tom has coined 'You-ie' as a word for 'selfie but of someone else' — a portmanteau that both makes sense and reveals his relentless branding instinct.
jokes.explanation: Tom inventing a word for 'selfie of someone else' is both absurd and internally logical. 'You-ie' is a good wordplay invention — it sounds like 'youie' (you + selfie) or 'u-ie' (a U-turn, itself a term Tom might appreciate). Highly Tom, quotable.

jokes.text: It's what I call selfies of other people.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Kay Hanley for a 'You-ie.'
jokes.punchline: Tom has coined 'You-ie' as his term for a selfie where the subject is someone else — a concept that is both logically coherent and completely redundant.
jokes.explanation: A solid Tom neologism joke. Tom's habit of branding everything with his own terminology is a recurring character beat, and 'You-ie' is a good invention — a selfie from someone else's perspective is just... a photo, and Tom doesn't see that. The calm explanation is perfect.

jokes.text: Our goal was to get 2,000 signatures in support of the merger. We got almost 4,000 on the first night!
jokes.setup: Andy announces the merger signature count.
jokes.punchline: The pause and crowd reaction to 4,000 — double the goal — is a warm moment, but Andy's delivery of 'almost 4,000' (qualifying the victory with 'almost') is a small funny beat.
jokes.explanation: More of a celebratory plot beat than a joke. The 'almost 4,000' qualifier is a minor Andy-ism. Weak comedy content but present.

jokes.text: 'Card one of six.' / Okay, I'm not reading this whole thing. Mr. Tom Haverford!
jokes.setup: Andy is given what appears to be a long, multi-card introduction speech for Tom.
jokes.punchline: After reading 'Card one of six,' Andy immediately abandons the prepared introduction and just says Tom's name.
jokes.explanation: A tight visual/character joke. The implication of a six-card Tom Haverford introduction (complete with his absurd self-branding quotes visible earlier) and Andy immediately giving up is a good bit. 'Card one of six' doing all the work.

jokes.text: Man, I'm gonna miss Pawnee. I wish I could stay. Keep an eye on it, raise my kids here. And let's be honest, am I ever gonna find a better breakfast than JJ's Diner? / You will not, no.
jokes.setup: Leslie is wistfully talking about what she'll miss about Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Ron's immediate, unqualified 'You will not, no' to the JJ's Diner question — the most Ron possible response to a sentimental moment.
jokes.explanation: Ron's single-minded agreement about the diner (rather than the sentiment) is perfectly in character. He processes the emotional moment through the food question and answers it with complete conviction. Good economy.

jokes.text: With your courage and small frame, you'd make an excellent coal miner.
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to encourage Leslie about her decision to take the new job.
jokes.punchline: Ron's sincere compliment pivots to 'you'd make an excellent coal miner' as an alternative — delivered with complete seriousness as high praise.
jokes.explanation: An excellent Ron Swanson joke. 'With your courage and small frame, you'd make an excellent coal miner' is a perfect fusion of sincere affection and Ron's warped frame of reference — where coal mining is a legitimate career compliment. The specificity of 'small frame' as a coal miner qualification is inspired. Deeply character-integrated and highly quotable.

jokes.text: And by the way, don't think that we are not discussing Duke Silver. When were you going to tell me about that? Unbelievable. I am so furious at you. But I've already forgiven you and you need to teach me how to play the saxophone. Okay, bye.
jokes.setup: Ron has just had a tender goodbye conversation with Leslie.
jokes.punchline: Leslie tacks on confrontation about Duke Silver — goes from fury to forgiveness to a saxophone lesson demand to 'okay, bye' in about four seconds.
jokes.explanation: A great escalating coda to a tender scene. Leslie's emotional processing goes through fury, forgiveness, practical demand (saxophone lessons), and abrupt exit all in one breath. The speed of emotional transit is the joke, and 'okay, bye' as the ending is perfect. Very Leslie.

jokes.text: Also, can you bring back Power Rangers? I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough to get that done.
jokes.setup: Ben has finished pitching Gryzzl's importance to Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Ben appends a personal Power Rangers revival request to the business pitch — treating the tech executive as a general-purpose influential person who might solve any problem.
jokes.explanation: A solid Ben nerd joke. 'I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough to get that done' is the perfect framing — Ben doesn't know Gryzzl's function but treats Power Rangers as a reasonable diplomatic ask. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: Also, can you bring back Power Rangers? I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough to get that done.
jokes.setup: Ben has just made an impressive pitch to the Gryzzl CEO about Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately asks the tech CEO to bring back Power Rangers — revealing his inner child and the limits of his professionalism.
jokes.explanation: Ben's nerd credentials showing at a business moment — using his leverage to pursue Power Rangers. The qualifier 'I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough' is a good additional character detail (Ben has no idea how tech companies work).

jokes.text: Sometimes you have to make the hardest climb to see the most beautiful sunrise. I read that once on an old lady's decorative pillow.
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering her confessional about her journey to a decision.
jokes.punchline: She cites an 'old lady's decorative pillow' as her philosophical source for what is clearly a sincere personal statement.
jokes.explanation: The sourcing of wisdom to a decorative pillow is a good Leslie beat — she finds inspiration everywhere, even tchotchkes. The sincerity with which she then says 'but it is really how I feel today' elevates it — she's not embarrassed by the source.

jokes.text: Ed, you're a nice guy, but you're the most incompetent person I've ever worked with. And that includes Terry. / Jeez. Get it together, Terry. / Clean out your desk. You're fired. / I understand. Thank you for the literally hundreds of opportunities you've given me.
jokes.setup: A flash-forward scene showing Leslie in a new, high-powered job in the future.
jokes.punchline: The reveal that Terry/Larry works for Leslie in her new job — and he's STILL the baseline for incompetence that others are compared against, despite not being fired. His gracious acceptance ('Thank you for the literally hundreds of opportunities') is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: A great tag scene that pays off the Larry running gag in a new context — Leslie's new office — while establishing that nothing has changed. 'That includes Terry' as the standard of incompetence, said in front of Terry, is very dark P&R humor. Larry's gracious 'literally hundreds of opportunities' is a perfect character response.

jokes.text: How many bags of marshmallows do I give them? / None. Just let April do everything.
jokes.setup: Andy is about to babysit Leslie and Ben's triplets.
jokes.punchline: The answer to 'how many marshmallows?' is 'none, just let April do everything' — which implies (1) April is the competent one between them, and (2) Ben has complete faith in April over Andy.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that tells us Ben trusts April (a goth who wanted to spit in people's food) more than Andy (a grown man asking about marshmallow quantities) with his children. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: Oh, God, one day in the distant future, things will be calm and normal, right? / Probably not. / But that's okay. / You ready? / Not at all. But that's never stopped us before.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are about to face a major meeting about their future.
jokes.punchline: The exchange validates chaos as normal for them — 'Probably not' and 'Not at all. But that's never stopped us before.' The romantic pragmatism is both touching and funny.
jokes.explanation: A warm closing beat that earns its humor through character relationship honesty. 'Probably not' to the question about things being calm is funny because it's said with such comfortable acceptance. Good economy in the exchange.

insight: Seventy jokes in 56 minutes, but character comedy carries a below-peak episode.
